9.1 State (Victorian) Impacts and Offset Requirements<|im_end|>
9.1.1 Removal, Destruction or Lopping of Native Vegetation (the Guidelines)<|im_end|>

The Guidelines (DELWP 2017) require offsetting as the final step in considering the impacts of development on native vegetation. Emphasis is placed on avoiding and minimising impacts, and only after these steps have been taken should offsets be considered.<|im_end|>

9.1.1.3 Offset Strategy<|im_end|>

According to DEECAs Native Vegetation Offset Register (DEECA 2025d), there are two offset sites within the Wimmera CMA that can be used to satisfy the General Habitat Unit and Large tree offset requirements, demonstrating that the offset obligation can be achieved should the project be approved.<|im_end|>
An offset register search statement identifying the relevant offsite sites is provided in Appendix 2.2.<|im_end|>
9.2 Commonwealth Offset Requirements<|im_end|>

The Australian Government's EPBC Act Environmental Offsets Policy (DSEWPaC 2012a) outlines a framework for the use of environmental offsets under the EPBC Act, including when they can be required, how they are determined and the framework under which they operate. Clear guidelines on what constitutes a suitable offset are provided and should be considered as part of any proposed offset strategy.<|im_end|>
Offsets to compensate for significant impacts to MNES will be provided in a manner consistent with the requirements of the EPBC Act Environmental Offsets Policy (DSEWPaC 2012a).<|im_end|>

Ecological surveys undertaken across multiple years identified the presence of several MNES (Section 5.1). Based on the proposed construction and operation of the project, there are proposed significant impacts to habitat for the nationally significant South-eastern Red-tail Black Cockatoo, and remnants of the Buloke Woodland ecological community (Figure 2; Figure 3).<|im_end|>
9.2.1 Matted Flax-lily<|im_end|>
9.2.1.1 Residual Impacts<|im_end|>
A total of approximately 60 Matted Flax-lily *Dianella amoena* colonies were recorded within the road reserve of Natimuk-Hamilton Road.<|im_end|>

The Disturbance Footprint has been designed to avoid all impacts to Matted Flax-lily specimens, with the new water pipeline connecting the mine to the Rocklands Douglas pipeline predominantly located within private property adjacent to Natimuk-Hamilton Road, with no specimens located where the pipeline crosses over the road reserve (Figure 2).<|im_end|>
9.2.1.2 Proposed Offsets<|im_end|>

As all Matted Flax-lily specimens are proposed to be retained as part of the project, there are not considered to be any impacts at a local, regional or national scale, and no offsets are proposed.<|im_end|>

9.2.2 Red-tailed Black Cockatoo<|im_end|>
9.2.2.1 Residual Impacts<|im_end|>

The Project Area is located at the north-eastern extent of the South-eastern Red-tail Black Cockatoo range, with Buloke seed providing a seasonal foraging resource over late summer and early autumn, and eucalypt-dominated woodlands providing roosting habitat for the species.<|im_end|>
Of the 1597 scattered trees and Large Trees proposed to be impacted, 1266 trees are identified as Buloke.<|im_end|>
A total of 22.747 hectares of foraging habitat in the form of Buloke-dominated Plains Woodland EVC, and 1126 scattered Buloke specimens are proposed to be impacted (Table 26; Table 27).<|im_end|>
No impacts are proposed to occur to potential roosting habitat recorded for the species around Red Gum Swamp, Darragan Swamp and the southern end of the pipeline alignment (Figure 2).<|im_end|>
9.2.2.2 Proposed Offsets<|im_end|>

The below offset scenario assumes that an offset site will be created at the property located at the corner of Cooks Lane and Natimuk-Hamilton Road, Noradjuha where preliminary assessments identified a large remnant of the Buloke Woodlands ecological community and scattered Buloke trees.<|im_end|>

Given detailed site surveys to determine habitat quality at the proposed offset site have not been completed at the date of this report, the habitat quality is assumed to be 4/10 for the purposes of this offset scenario.<|im_end|>

9.2.3 Growling Grass Frog<|im_end|>
9.2.3.1 Proposed Impacts<|im_end|>

Between 2-4 Growling Grass Frog were heard calling at Darragan Swamp during the 2022 breeding season. No Growling Grass Frog were recorded at any of the other seven wetlands investigated during the survey effort, and based on the location of existing records, the results of the other targeted surveys and condition of overall potential habitat, it is considered highly unlikely that any other resident populations of the species is present or relies on habitat within the Project Area, or is able to access additional habitat within the Project Area if it is not already present.<|im_end|>
Indirect impacts such as changes to water quality, quantity and hydrology as a result of the proposed project may negatively impact this population of Growling Grass Frog.<|im_end|>

Darragan Swamp is an ephemeral wetland that fills regularly and draws down relatively quickly, with water sourced from direct catchment runoff without any connection to river floodplain flows (Water Technology 2025). It is located outside the proposed development footprint, approximately 6 kilometres north-east of Jallumba Marsh.<|im_end|>

Modelling indicates that Darragan Swamp routinely drops from full or near full to near empty or dry within 1-2 years. The modelling also predicts that Darragan Swamp experiences more regular dry periods, with these periods being quite short and occur on average once every 5 years (Water Technology 2025). Darragan Swamp has a clearly defined outlet channel heading north from the northern end of the wetland. The depth of the wetland is only  $0.9\mathrm{m}$  and the results show that the wetland storage reaches capacity quite often and spills to downstream receptors at least every one to two years on average, with water levels in the swamp primarily driven by inflow during the wet season in each year, rather than a result of a prolonged multi-year wet period (Water Technology 2025)<|im_end|>

An analysis of potential impacts to Darragan Swamp found that the wetland will be impacted from early in the mine life with activities scheduled to start from the northern areas resulting in a reduction in catchment area caused by the mine reducing inflows (Water Technology 2025). However, the reduction in inflows is relatively minor and does not significantly alter the hydraulic regime of wetland given that Darragan fills regularly and draws down relatively quickly, and the reduced inflows are unlikely to change the ecological character of the wetland.<|im_end|>

However, the installation of supplementary pipeline infrastructure is proposed to enable delivery of supplementary water to mitigate any potential hydrological impact to the wetland and ensure that the current hydrological regime is maintained to ensure the suitability of Darragan Swamp as breeding and foraging habitat for Growling Grass Frog is not compromised.<|im_end|>
9.2.3.2 Proposed Offsets<|im_end|>

Provided the Wetland Watering Plan (Water Technology 2025) is implemented to ensure that the suitability of Darragan Swamp as a breeding site for Growling Grass Frog is maintained, and the inundation regime that would have occurred pre-mining is maintained in a post-mining scenario (with reference to seasonal conditions within the region), no impacts to Growling Grass Frog are assumed, and no offsets are proposed.<|im_end|>

9.2.6 Seasonal Herbaceous Wetlands (Freshwater) of the Temperate Lowland Plains.<|im_end|>
9.2.6.1 Proposed Impacts<|im_end|>

The nationally significant community Seasonal Herbaceous Wetlands (Freshwater) of the Temperate Lowland Plains (SHW community) is present in one large patch totalling an area of 22.434 hectares located within Jallumba Marsh Flora Reserve.<|im_end|>

Based on the current Disturbance Footprint, a total of 0.05 hectares of the SHW community will be impacted as a result of an internal road proposed to be constructed adjacent to Jallumba Marsh Flora Reserve (Figure 2a-vii). The next iteration of the Disturbance Footprint will be amended to avoid impacts to the Seasonal Herbaceous Wetlands (Freshwater) of the Temperate Lowland Plain ecological community.<|im_end|>
Indirect impacts such as changes to water quality, quantity and hydrology as a result of the proposed project may negatively impact the community, and result in a significant impact.<|im_end|>

An assessment of potential indirect impacts to the Jallumba Marsh Flora Reserve found that a water reduction will occur, although is modelled to correlate with wetter years only (Water Technology 2025). However, this impact can be minimised through the relocation of stockpiles to restore runoff from the unaffected catchment that feeds Jallumba Marsh Flora Reserve from this direction, and as such, no supplementary watering would be required to maintain the existing values present (i.e. SHW community).<|im_end|>
Based on the results of the hydrological analysis undertaken by Water Technology (2025), no indirect impacts are assumed to occur to the SHW community.<|im_end|>
9.2.6.2 Proposed Offsets<|im_end|>
The existing proposed impact of 0.05 hectares is not considered to be a significant impact to the ecological community, and no offsets are proposed.<|im_end|>

However, it is recommended that Iluka review the internal road alignment that is located directly adjacent to the SHW community to ensure no impact occurs. Further, a buffer should be implemented between the Disturbance Footprint to mitigate against indirect impacts to the community during construction and operation of the project. Further review of potential impacts and offsets associated with the SHW community will be undertaken as preparation of the Wetland Watering Plan (Water Technology 2025) progresses, and further iterations to the Disturbance Footprint occur.<|im_end|>
